Base directory for this skill: /Users/omshukla/.commandcode/skills/scope

## Output style (plain words, no dashes, no hyphens)

<!-- OUTPUT-STYLE:START -->
Write everything this skill produces, files and messages alike, in plain simple language. Talk to the reader as `you`, warm and direct like a colleague, and present every step as a recommendation they may run or skip, never an order. Keep technical terms that carry real meaning; explain each in plain words. Never use a dash or a hyphen as punctuation: no em dash, no en dash, and no hyphenated compounds. Write `read only`, not `read-only`. Say it in simple words, or reword the sentence. Code, file paths, command flags, and values other skills match on keep their hyphens. Use short sentences, commas, or parentheses. Clear beats clever.
<!-- OUTPUT-STYLE:END -->

## What this skill does

Turns an idea into an ordered, coarse, living plan and keeps it honest as the product ships. Answers what to build, in what order, how heavy, which need a decision first, not how to build one thing (that is `/architect` and `/develop`).

Scope shape, coarse and small: a slim At a glance table (`# · Feature · Phase · Status`) + feature sections grouped by phase (see `scope-template.md`). Each section: heading `### N. Name` with short tags only when they matter (`needs a decision`, an approach override, a workflow tier override like `· GA`), a 1 to 2 line intent, one `Done when:` line (acceptance criteria seeds, the WHAT), checkbox steps.

Feature shape lifecycle: not yet designed → one box, its entry command. On spec capture, `/architect` fills the built ready shape: `Design it (spec)` ticked, spec linked, `Build it: /develop <feature>` with 2 to 5 milestone sub items rolled up from the spec's `## Build plan`, then `Verify it: /check verify <feature>` and `Test it: /test <feature>`. Atomic build tasks stay in the spec's `## Build plan`, never here; every box is a command or tracked milestone. Status: in the table and beside the heading; spec and code pointers once they exist.

One command, inferred intent (`/scope [what]`, never a subcommand):
- **plan** (default): no scope yet + a product sized idea, or asking for the next slice. Full pass: ask → decompose into coarse feature sections → order + phase → write.
- **replan**: scope exists + no argument. Opens with a short where things stand readout (git branch and ahead/behind the remote, feature counts by status, and each in-progress feature's resume point) so a bare `/scope` doubles as the "where was I, what is safe to pick up" orientation, then reconciles what shipped, surfaces plan vs reality drift (code or specs with no scope row), enrolls needs surfaced during the build, reorders, and queues the next slice. The normal living rhythm, not rare: run bare `/scope` again.
- **add**: scope exists + argument names a single feature. Enroll one coarse row (intent + order + tier + Needs spec) without planning again: `/scope <a feature>`.

## Asks vs acts

Senior product engineer. Same infer / ask / recommend discipline as `/architect`: INFER what the idea states (category, obvious capabilities); ASK what cannot be inferred across business, product, go to market in batched rounds (up to 4 questions per round; see Decision panels); RECOMMEND build approach, build order, the workflow tier (project default and any per feature override), which need a spec (expert calls: present them, let the engineer override).

Never pick tools: no provider, library, ORM, host, or BaaS chosen or named; that is `/architect`'s job per feature in the spec. A feature implying a tool choice is exactly `Needs spec: yes`. Keep the scope tool agnostic so it doesn't rot.

## Decision panels (every user facing choice)

Every choice is an options panel, never a neutral menu: 2 to 4 concrete options real to this product; exactly one marked `(recommended)` with a one line why (make the call, let them override). Never add your own Other option, the picker appends a free text Other automatically; offer free text yourself only in a plain text fallback with no picker. Capability first: use the agent's picker (`AskUserQuestion` on Claude Code), else the same options as plain text; batched rounds same rule, up to 4 per round.

## Artifact ownership

`docs/scope/` is the feature scope, owned by this skill; `/architect` owns `docs/specs/`. Other skills find a feature by scanning `docs/scope/` for its row. Living document: `plan`, `replan`, `add` all edit in place (reconcile and append, never a new dated file). Writes nothing else: no specs, code, or `AGENTS.md`. `docs/scope/` holds scope files only; inventories, analyses, research docs live with the spec in its `rationale.md` (owned by `/architect`).

File shape:
- Small product: one file, `docs/scope/scope.md` (At a glance table + phase grouped sections + legend).
- Large product: epic split: `docs/scope/index.md` (At a glance table across epics + one line status rollup per epic, each linking its epic file) + one file per epic named by area (`docs/scope/auth.md`, …).
- Promote on demand: start single file; when `scope.md` outgrows a comfortable scan (roughly a dozen plus features across clearly distinct areas), rename to `index.md` (keep table + per epic rollup), move each area's sections into its own `<epic>.md`. Never split it early. Names semantic (`scope.md` / `index.md` / `<epic>.md`), never numbered.
- Keep every file coarse and small; a long epic file needs finer features and tighter intent, not a build task dump.

Status lifecycle (`/scope` sets initial status; the pipeline advances it):
- New features start `planned`. Brownfield: also enroll features that are already there as `existing` (complete) or `in-progress` (partial), the only other statuses `/scope` writes.
- `/develop` advances pipeline built work (`planned` → `in-progress` → `done`); `/sync` reconciles against the diff. A feature built on an **assumed decision** (its governing spec is `Assumed`, recorded by `/develop` when the engineer chose to build before deciding) carries an `assumed decision (spec NNNN)` note until `/architect` ratifies the decision; the note does not block `done`, it is decision debt that stays surfaced until ratified.
- `done` ≠ `existing`: `done` = this pipeline built and verified it; `existing` predates the workflow; `/develop` and `/sync` never touch `existing` rows.
- `replan` may set a feature dropped from scope to `dropped`, never deletes rows; `dropped` keeps history, excluded from active counts and work; `/develop` and `/sync` skip it.

Workflow tier (one rigor dial per feature, `Prototype` · `Alpha` · `Beta` · `GA`): how much process a feature warrants. ONE project default (recommended once, plan Step 5b, recorded on the scope header `**Workflow:**` line) and a per feature override (a tag beside the heading, e.g. `· GA`, only when a feature differs from the default; no tag = inherit). What the tier drives:
- **Design time**: higher tier → more likely `Needs spec: yes`, and the spec's cross model decision critic runs (auto at `GA`/`Beta`). `Prototype`/`Alpha` features are often `Needs spec: no`.
- **After `/develop`** (the verification tail): `Prototype` = nothing (rely on `/develop`'s own build time self check); `Alpha` = `/check verify`; `Beta` = `/check verify` + `/test`; `GA` = adds a fresh model `/check review` + `/document`.
- **What closes `done`** (the last required stage marks it): `Prototype` → `/develop` (build + self check); `Alpha` → `/check verify`; `Beta`/`GA` → `/test`. An `Assumed` spec never blocks `done`; it stays flagged as owing ratification (`/architect`) at every tier.

`/scope` recommends the project default from the risk and size of the feature mix (Step 5b), the same signals `/architect` and `/develop` read; `/develop` reads the effective tier (feature override, else project default, else inferred) to scale the next steps it recommends, so a `Prototype` project is not told to run verify and a `Alpha` project is not told to run a full review chain.

Artifact base: `docs/` by default; if `docs/` is a published docs site (`docusaurus.config.*`, `.vitepress/`, `mkdocs.yml`, Astro Starlight, or Nextra detected), use `.workflow/` (`.workflow/scope/…`). Always follow whichever base already exists (paths here assume `docs/`).

Concurrency: shared across sessions and teammates. Read again immediately before writing; surgical edits only (append rows in order, reconcile changed cells, never rewrite the file); flag rather than clobber unexpected state; append with the next free numbers so adders don't collide.

## Reference files

- `scope-template.md`: format rules, At a glance table, per feature sections (heading + intent + Done when + checkbox tasks + pointer line), brownfield enrollment and epic split shapes, the `## /scope complete` report block. Read it when writing the scope and the report.

## Portability (any OS, any agent)

Any Agent Skills client on macOS, Linux, Windows. Detection snippets are POSIX reference; use your agent's cross platform file tools. Planning runs inline; the two subagents below (Step 1 brownfield code scan, Step 6b sourcing) are optional and capability first, degrade to inline. No interactive picker: ask every panel as plain text, same options.

## Execution

### Step 0: Infer intent & idea check

No subcommand. First check whether a scope exists under `docs/scope/` (or `.workflow/scope/` if that is the artifact base), then infer:
- Scope exists + no argument (or running again, described as "reconcile / what's next") → replan behavior (`modes/replan.md`).
- Scope exists + argument names a single feature → add behavior (`modes/add.md`).
- No scope yet + a product sized idea, or scoping the next slice (including brownfield) → plan behavior, below.

Ambiguous (a new slice vs a single feature): infer the most likely reading from scope, say which behavior you chose in the report; truly unclear → one line clarifying question.

Plan behavior, no idea given (no argument, no scope to extend): stop and ask before anything else:

"What are you building? Describe the product or the slice of it you want to plan (one or two sentences about what it does and who it's for)."

Wait for the answer; use it as the product idea.

### Step 1: Load the inferred behavior

After Step 0 infers the behavior, read exactly one mode file and follow it:

- `modes/plan.md` for plan behavior (new scope, product sized idea, or next slice planning).
- `modes/replan.md` for replan behavior (scope exists and no argument).
- `modes/add.md` for add behavior (scope exists and the argument names one feature).

Do not read the other mode files unless the inferred behavior changes. All common rules above still apply, and `scope-template.md` remains the format reference for any write/report.

1: FileSure - Tech assignment
2: 
3: Thank you for applying to FileSure.
4: 
5: FileSure (filesure.in) holds the official records of every Indian company and LLP: master data, directors, financials, filings and the original MCA documents. A small team builds it with the best AI tools available.
6: 
7: Use AI. We expect it. Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Copilot, anything you like. We are not testing whether you can work without AI. We are testing how well you work with it: how you prompt it, how you check it, and what you make with it.
8: 
9: There is one task. It takes about 3 hours. Send everything within 72 hours to the email this came from.
10: 
11: The task: build a CIN checker
12: 
13: Every Indian company has a 21-character Corporate Identity Number (CIN), for example L17110MH1973PLC019786. Every LLP has an LLPIN, for example AAA-1234.
14: 
15: Build a web page where someone pastes a list of CINs and LLPINs, one per line, and gets back what each one means:
16: • valid or not (and if not, exactly what is wrong)
17: • company or LLP
18: • listed or unlisted
19: • state
20: • year of incorporation
21: • company type (public, private, one-person company, government company, ...)
22: 
23: Research the CIN format yourself. Then put the page online on any free host (GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify, ...).
24: 
25: Design counts as much as the code. Design it as if it were going live on filesure.in tomorrow, for CAs, lawyers and business owners. We will judge:
26: • how clear and pleasant it is to use, the first time, with no instructions
27: • layout, typography, spacing and colour
28: • how it looks and works on a phone as well as on a laptop
29: • what it shows when the input is empty, wrong, or 500 lines long
30: 
31: What to send
32: 1. Live link to the page.
33: 2. Code repository (public GitHub link).
34: 3. Your full AI transcripts, every conversation you had with AI for this task, unedited. We read them to see how you prompt. For example:
35:    • Claude Code: run /export in each session, or send the .jsonl files from ~/.claude/projects/
36:    • Claude.ai or ChatGPT: share links to the chats
37:    • Cursor or another editor: export the chat history
38: 4. A video, 10 minutes or less: your screen, face and voice. Show the page working, explain one design decision you are proud of, walk through the code, and show at least one place the AI got something wrong and how you caught it.
39: 
40: Without the transcripts and the video, the assignment is not reviewed.
41: 
42: The next round: live, with your AI tools
43: 
44: If we shortlist you, we meet for 30 minutes on a video call. You share your screen, and we ask you to change something in your own page, live, using whatever AI tools you like, while you talk us through it.
45: 
46: What we look at
47: • Does it work? We will paste in tricky inputs.
48: • Is it well designed? Would a first-time visitor understand it and enjoy it?
49: • How do you prompt? Clear asks, good context, steering the AI when it goes wrong, not just accepting its first answer.
50: • Do you understand what you built? Can you explain it simply?

# State Codes and CIN Format Guide – How to Read a CIN Number
## What is a CIN?
A **CIN (Corporate Identification Number)** is a **21-character alphanumeric code** assigned by the **Registrar of Companies (ROC)** to every company incorporated in India under the Companies Act. It is issued at the time of incorporation and mentioned in the **Certificate of Incorporation**.
**> Important
**> : CIN is issued to
**> companies
**> only.
**> Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs)
**> are issued a
**> LLPIN (LLP Identification Number)
**> – a 7-character alphanumeric code.
### Where is CIN Used?
Every company must quote its CIN on:
* Letterheads, billheads, and letter papers
* Notices, invoices, and official publications
* All forms and filings submitted to MCA
* Email communications
* Any other external communication
**Non-compliance penalty**: ₹1,000 per day for the defaulting company and every officer in default, subject to a maximum of ₹1,00,000.
## CIN Format – How to Read It
A CIN consists of **6 distinct parts**, each conveying specific information about the company:
```
Example CIN: L 01631 KA 2010 PTC 096843
             ↑ ↑↑↑↑↑ ↑↑ ↑↑↑↑ ↑↑↑ ↑↑↑↑↑↑
            [1] [2] [3] [4]  [5] [6]
```
|Part|Position|Type|Length|What It Represents|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|1|1st character|Alpha|1|**Listing Status**|
|2|2nd–6th character|Numeric|5|**Industry/Economic Activity Code**|
|3|7th–8th character|Alpha|2|**State Code**|
|4|9th–12th character|Numeric|4|**Year of Incorporation**|
|5|13th–15th character|Alpha|3|**Company Type**|
|6|16th–21st character|Numeric|6|**ROC Registration Number**|
## Part 1 – Listing Status (1 Character)
The first character indicates whether the company is listed on a stock exchange:
|Code|Meaning|
|---|---|
|**L**|Listed on a recognized stock exchange in India|
|**U**|Unlisted company|
## Part 2 – Industry / Economic Activity Code (5 Digits)
The 5-digit numeric code represents the **primary economic activity** of the company. This is derived from the **[NIC Code](https://learn.cspratik.com/docs/other-resources/nic-code-2008/) (National Industrial Classification)** system maintained by MCA.
Some commonly encountered industry codes:

[> NIC Code 2008 resource](https://learn.cspratik.com/docs/other-resources/nic-code-2008/)> on this website.
## Part 3 – State Code (2 Characters)
The state code indicates the **state where the company’s registered office is located** and, consequently, the **ROC (Registrar of Companies)** under which it is registered:

|**AN**|Andaman and Nicobar Islands|ROC – Andaman & Nicobar|

|**UT**|Uttarakhand|ROC – Kanpur|
|**WB**|West Bengal|ROC – Kolkata I / ROC - Kolkata II|
## Part 4 – Year of Incorporation (4 Digits)
This is simply the **4-digit year** in which the company was incorporated. For example, `2010` means the company was incorporated in the year 2010.
## Part 5 – Company Type (3 Characters)
The 3-character alpha code represents the **legal type** of the company:
|Code|Company Type|
|---|---|
|**PLC**|Public Limited Company|
|**PTC**|Private Limited Company|
|**OPC**|One Person Company|
|**NPL**|Not-for-Profit / Section 8 Company|
|**FLC**|Financial Leasing Company|
|**FTC**|Subsidiary of a Foreign Company (Foreign Subsidiary)|
|**GAP**|General Association – Public|
|**GAT**|General Association – Private|
|**GOI**|Government of India Company|
|**SGC**|State Government Company|
|**ULL**|Public Limited Company with Unlimited Liability|
|**ULT**|Private Limited Company with Unlimited Liability|
## Part 6 – Registration Number (6 Digits)
The final 6-digit number is the **unique sequential registration number** assigned by the ROC at the time of incorporation. This, combined with the state code (Part 3), uniquely identifies the company within the ROC’s records.
## Decoding a CIN – Practical Example
Let us decode the CIN: **U74900DL2015PTC282029**
|Part|Value|Meaning|
|---|---|---|
|Listing Status|**U**|Unlisted company|
|Industry Code|**74900**|Other professional, scientific and technical activities|
|State Code|**DL**|Delhi|
|Year|**2015**|Incorporated in 2015|
|Company Type|**PTC**|Private Limited Company|
|Registration No.|**282029**|ROC registration number|
**Reading**: This is an **unlisted private limited company** incorporated in **Delhi in 2015**, engaged in **professional services**, bearing ROC registration number 282029.
## What is LLPIN?
For **Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs)**, the equivalent of CIN is the **LLPIN (LLP Identification Number)**. It is a **7-character alphanumeric code** in the format: **AAA-0000** (e.g., AAA-1234).
The LLPIN does not encode the same level of information as a CIN. It is a sequential number issued by the ROC.
> LLPs do not have a listing status, industry code, or state code embedded in their identification number.
## When Does a CIN Change?
A company’s CIN changes when there is a structural change in the company that alters any of the encoded elements:
* **Change in listing status** (company gets listed or delisted) → First character changes from U to L or vice versa
* **Change in company type** (e.g., private to public conversion) → Part 5 changes (PTC → PLC)
* **Change in state of registered office** (cross-state transfer) → State code changes
The year of incorporation and registration number do not change.

I've read the assignment, the PDF, and researched the CIN format plus FileSure's own site. Here is what you are walking into.

## What they are asking you to make

One page. A person pastes a list of company and LLP identifiers, one per line, and the page tells them what each one means. No login, no accounts, no database in the request. A box in, a decoded list out. Then you put it on a free host and send a link.

That is the whole product. Everything else is how well you do it.

## What the two identifiers actually are

**CIN (Corporate Identity Number)** is 21 characters, fixed order, and every block means something:

```
L 17110 MH 1973 PLC 019786
│ │     │  │    │   └── 6 digits: serial number the ROC gave it
│ │     │  │    └────── 3 letters: company type
│ │     │  └─────────── 4 digits: year of incorporation
│ │     └────────────── 2 letters: state of registered office
│ └──────────────────── 5 digits: industry code (NIC, the main activity)
└────────────────────── 1 letter: L listed, U unlisted
```

So a CIN is a self describing code. Reading it needs no lookup service, just the tables behind each block. That is the insight the whole task hangs on.

The three letter company type is the block most people get wrong. The common ones:

- `PTC` private limited, `PLC` public limited, `OPC` one person company
- `NPL` Not for Profit, Section 8 company
- `FTC` subsidiary of a foreign company
- `GOI` central government company, `SGC` state government company
- `ULL` and `ULT` unlimited liability variants
- `GAP` and `GAT` older general association codes, `FLC` financial leasing

**LLPIN** is the trap. It is seven characters, `AAA-1234`, three letters, a hyphen, four digits. It is a pure serial number. It carries no state, no year, no listing status and no company type, and the assignment only asks you to say it is an LLP. Anyone who tries to decode an LLPIN the way they decode a CIN is wrong, and saying that out loud in the interview shows you did the research.

## What "valid" has to mean

This is where the checker lives or dies. Validity is not "looks about right". Each position has a rule:

1. Exactly 21 characters, no spaces inside, no hyphen.
2. First character `L` or `U` only.
3. Positions 2 to 6 are digits.
4. Positions 7 and 8 are a real MCA state code (`MH`, `DL`, `KA`, `TG`, `OR`, `CG`, `UT` and so on).
5. Positions 9 to 12 are a plausible year, not in the future, not before company law.
6. Positions 13 to 15 are a known company type code.
7. Positions 16 to 21 are six digits.

And the failure message has to name the exact break: "state code `XX` is not a valid MCA state", not "invalid CIN".

Two real world wrinkles worth knowing, because they make you look like you did the homework:

- **Odisha is `OR`, not `OD`.** People assume `OD` from the state abbreviation and get it wrong.
- **Telangana is `TG`.** Companies incorporated there before the 2014 split carry `AP` and MCA later reissued them as `TG`. Both are worth accepting.
- **Old and merged territories**: `DD` Daman and Diu and `DN` Dadra and Nagar Haveli still appear, even though the two merged into one territory.
- **Leading zeros matter.** The last six digits are often `019786` or `000123`. Stripping them breaks it.

## How the person actually interacts with it

1. Land on the page. One line says what it does. One example CIN is visible so they can copy it and try.
2. Paste into a box. Live checking as they paste is better than a button, but a button is fine if it feels instant.
3. Results appear under the box. For each line: the code itself, a badge saying valid, invalid, or LLP, then one plain sentence ("Unlisted private limited company, incorporated in Maharashtra in 1973") and then the decoded blocks laid out as labeled values.
4. For an invalid line, the message points at the broken block and says what was expected.
5. On a phone it is one column, the box is full width, the results stack.

The three states they said they will judge:

- **Empty**: should teach, not sit blank. Short explanation plus a working example they can click.
- **Wrong**: precise, calm, not red screaming. "Character 7 and 8 should be a state code. `ZZ` is not one."
- **500 lines**: must stay fast and readable. That means parsing instantly, showing a count summary at the top, and a way to see only the broken ones.

## The thing I would tell them in the interview

This page should run entirely in the browser, with no server and no database. Reasons that are strong and true:

- The output is fully determined by the input, so a server adds nothing but a round trip.
- CAs and lawyers paste client identifiers. Saying "nothing you paste leaves your browser" is a real trust feature, and it is only true if there is no backend.
- 500 lines parse in milliseconds locally. Over a network it is slower and can fail.
- Nothing to store means nothing to breach.

If you were planning MongoDB and a Node server for this, I would push back on that: a reviewer may read it as not understanding the problem. The honest shape is a static site.

input.content:
# Scope: CIN Checker (FileSure tech assignment)

A single page where a CA, a lawyer or a business owner pastes a list of Indian company and LLP identifiers, one per line, and gets back what each one means: valid or not, company or LLP, listed or unlisted, state, year of incorporation and company type. Built to look and read as if it went live on filesure.in tomorrow.

**Build approach:** Skateboard (ship the smallest usable whole, then grow the same page release by release).
**Workflow:** Alpha (/check verify after /develop). The decoder carries a `· Beta` tag so it also gets a real test suite, because that is where the reviewer's tricky inputs land. `/architect` is the recommended first stop for a feature with a real decision, but skippable when you already know the build. Any feature can carry its own tag to do more or less.

_These are recommendations to keep your build orderly, not requirements. Skip anything that does not fit: if you already know how to build a feature, use `/develop` and skip `/architect`. You decide when a feature is `done`._

## At a glance

| # | Feature | Phase | Status |
|---|---------|-------|--------|
| 1 | Stack & architecture | Foundation | planned |
| 2 | Coding standards & tooling | Foundation | planned |
| 3 | Decode rules & reference data | Foundation | planned |
| 4 | Design system & UI foundation | Foundation | planned |
| 5 | Decoder & test suite | Slice 1 | planned |
| 6 | Checker page & results | Slice 1 | planned |
| 7 | Working with long lists | Slice 2 | planned |
| 8 | Download results as CSV | Slice 2 | planned |
| 9 | Shareable link | Slice 3 | planned |
| 10 | Empty, wrong and extreme states | Slice 3 | planned |
| 11 | Ship it and submit | Slice 4 | planned |

## Foundations

### 1. Stack & architecture · needs a decision
Decide how the page is built and scaffold a runnable project so every later slice stands on real structure. One decision worth defending out loud: this page needs no server and no database, because the answer is fully determined by the text the visitor pastes, so a static build answers in under a millisecond, works on any free host, and lets you say honestly that nothing pasted ever leaves the browser.
**Done when:** the spec records the stack and the "no server, no database" call with its reasoning, and the empty scaffold boots locally and passes a production build.
- [ ] Decide the stack (spec): `/architect stack & architecture`

### 2. Coding standards & tooling
Capture the conventions the assignment is judged on (readable code you can explain simply) and install the guards so every later file follows them, from the real scaffold.
**Done when:** root `AGENTS.md` reflects the real stack, and lint, format and type checking run clean on the scaffold.
- [ ] Capture conventions + tooling choices: `/audit`
- [ ] Install the tooling: `/develop tooling`
- [ ] Check it runs clean: `/check verify tooling`

### 3. Decode rules & reference data · needs a decision
The one place the domain rules live, because guessing here is what makes a checker wrong. Decides the exact block layout of a CIN, the full table of MCA state codes, the full table of company type codes, how NIC industry digits are described (or deliberately left unexplained), the LLPIN pattern, and the shape of one parsed result plus its error reasons. Everything in slices 1 to 3 rests on this.
**Done when:** the spec carries the state table, the type table and the error reason list, each entry traceable to a source, and states plainly what an LLPIN can and cannot tell you.
- [ ] Design it (spec): `/architect decode rules & reference data`

### 4. Design system & UI foundation · needs a decision
Match FileSure's own visual language so the page argues it already belongs on filesure.in, and decide the two result layouts (cards for a short paste, a table for a long one) before either is built. Owns type scale, spacing, colour, badges for valid, invalid and LLP, and the base components.
**Done when:** `design.md` covers type, colour, spacing, the two result layouts and their switch point, and the base components handle focus, keyboard and a phone width.
- [ ] Design it (spec): `/architect design system & UI foundation`

## Slice 1: The smallest usable whole

### 5. Decoder & test suite · Beta
Turn one line of text into a typed result: which kind it is, and for a CIN every block decoded or the exact reason it breaks. Pure logic with no screen attached, so it can be tested against the tricky inputs a reviewer will try.
**Done when:** a test suite proves valid CINs decode every field, each malformed block yields its own named error, LLPINs are recognised, and messy paste habits (extra spaces, mixed case, trailing punctuation, invisible characters) are cleaned before checking.
- [ ] Build it: `/develop decoder & test suite`
- [ ] Test it: `/test decoder & test suite`

### 6. Checker page & results
The page itself: a paste box, live results under it, and each result opening with one plain sentence a non expert understands, then the decoded blocks as labelled values. Cards for a short paste, table for a long one, one column on a phone.
**Done when:** a first time visitor can paste a list with no instructions and read every answer, each invalid line says which block failed and what was expected, and the phone layout is usable at 360 pixels wide.
- [ ] Build it: `/develop checker page & results`
- [ ] Verify it: `/check verify checker page & results`

## Slice 2: Real client files

### 7. Working with long lists · needs a decision
Five hundred lines is called out in the brief, and five hundred rich cards will make a browser crawl. Decide how the page stays fast and readable at that size, then add the summary strip and the filter that makes a big paste actionable.
**Done when:** pasting 500 lines stays responsive while scrolling and typing, a summary shows how many were valid, invalid and LLP, and one control hides the valid ones without losing the counts.
- [ ] Design it (spec): `/architect working with long lists`

### 8. Download results as CSV
Let a visitor take the decoded list into a spreadsheet, which is how a CA actually files client work.
**Done when:** one button downloads a CSV with a header row and one row per pasted line, messy values are quoted safely, and the file opens correctly in Excel and in Numbers.
- [ ] Build it: `/develop download results as CSV`
- [ ] Verify it: `/check verify download results as CSV`

## Slice 3: Share and polish

### 9. Shareable link
Encode the pasted list into the URL so a colleague opening the link sees the same results, with a sane cap so long lists never produce a broken link.
**Done when:** opening a share link restores the list and its results, a list beyond the cap shares a clear message instead of a truncated link, and no pasted data is sent anywhere to make it work.
- [ ] Build it: `/develop shareable link`
- [ ] Verify it: `/check verify shareable link`

### 10. Empty, wrong and extreme states
The brief names these three states as judged, so treat them as designed screens rather than leftovers: an empty page that teaches with a working example, a wrong input that stays calm and specific, and an enormous paste that stays readable.
**Done when:** the empty state offers a one click example, a single garbage line explains what was expected without an alarm, and a 500 line paste shows a summary rather than a wall of red.
- [ ] Build it: `/develop empty, wrong and extreme states`
- [ ] Verify it: `/check verify empty, wrong and extreme states`

## Slice 4: Submit

### 11. Ship it and submit
The brief says an entry is not reviewed without these, so they are part of the product, not an afterthought.
**Done when:** the live URL loads on a phone and a laptop, the repo is public with a short README that explains the decode rules, the AI transcripts are exported unedited, and the ten minute video covers a working demo, one design decision, a code walkthrough and one place the AI was wrong and how it was caught.
- [ ] Deploy to a free host and check the live link: `/develop ship it and submit`
- [ ] Export transcripts, record the video, send the email: `/develop ship it and submit`

## Deferred
Out of scope for today, kept so the plan stays honest and so you have something to say when the interviewer asks what you would do next.
- **Live lookup against MCA records**: confirm the CIN exists and pull the real company name, not just decode the digits. Needs a decision. This is the honest boundary of what a decoder can claim.
- **Bulk clean up and fix suggestions**: offer to correct near misses like `OD` for `OR` or a stray space. Needs a decision.
- **Saved history for repeat visitors**: remember recent lists in the browser. Needs a decision.

A **Corporate Identification Number** (**CIN**) is a 21-digit [alpha-numeric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphanumericals) code issued to companies incorporated in India. CIN[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) is unique identification number that is given by [Registrar of Companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registrar_of_Companies_(India)) (ROC) of various states under the [Ministry of Corporate Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Corporate_Affairs) (MCA). CINs are assigned to companies registered in India by the ROC located in states across the nation.
## Structure
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corporate_Identification_Number&action=edit&section=1)]
CIN have 21 alpha-numeric characters. CIN can be broken down in six sections. Example of CIN issued by ROC– L01631KA2010PTC096843
* Section-1: The listing status
* Section-2: The industry code
* Section-3: The state code
* Section-4: The year of incorporation
* Section-5: The ownership
* Section-6: The registration number
## Importance
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corporate_Identification_Number&action=edit&section=2)]
CIN is used for tracking all the aspects and activities of a [company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company) from its incorporation by the ROC and is required to be provided on all the transactions with the respective ROC.

content.text:
The scope is written and all five reference links are confirmed by fetching them directly. Here is the briefing you asked for, then the plan.

## What they are asking you to make

One page. No login, no accounts, no database required. Someone pastes a list of company and LLP identifiers, one per line, and the page tells them what each one means. Then you host it free and send a link.

The product is tiny. The grading is not. They score design as heavily as code, and they will paste deliberately awkward input to see if it breaks.

## What the identifiers actually are

**CIN** is 21 characters, fixed order, every block self describing:

```
L 17110 MH 1973 PLC 019786
│ │     │  │    │   └── 6 digits: ROC serial number
│ │     │  │    └────── 3 letters: company type
│ │     │  └─────────── 4 digits: year of incorporation
│ │     └────────────── 2 letters: state of registered office
│ └──────────────────── 5 digits: NIC industry code
└────────────────────── 1 letter: L listed, U unlisted
```

That Reliance example is real and it is the one FileSure themselves show. It decodes as a listed public limited company, incorporated in Maharashtra in 1973, in textiles, serial 019786. Memorise that string, it makes you look fluent.

**LLPIN** is the trap they will test. Seven characters, `AAA-1234`, three letters, hyphen, four digits. It is a pure serial. It carries no state, no year, no listing status, no company type. The brief only asks you to say "it is an LLP". If a candidate invents a state for an LLPIN, that is a fail. Say clearly that an LLPIN cannot be decoded further, and that is a win.

## The single most important thing to say in the interview

A format check is not an existence check.

A CIN can be perfectly well formed and still belong to no company. Your page proves the digits are internally consistent with MCA rules. It does not prove the company exists. MCA's own portal says "CIN is invalid" for codes that are structurally fine but not on the register.

Say that sentence unprompted and you separate yourself from everyone who built a regex. It also explains why there is no database: the truth about existence lives at MCA, not in your app. Mention that live lookup is the obvious next step, which is already sitting in your Deferred list.

## How the client actually interacts with it

1. Land on the page. One line says what it does, one example CIN is visible so a stranger can click and try.
2. Paste. Results appear as they type, no submit button needed.
3. Each result opens with one plain sentence a business owner understands, then the blocks as labelled values. Cards for a short paste, a table for a long one.
4. Each bad line names the broken block and what was expected, not a blanket "invalid".
5. On a phone it is one column, full width box, results stacked.

## The tricky inputs they will try

Have an answer ready for each of these:

- **Lowercase or extra spaces**: `l17110mh1973plc019786` or `L17110 MH1973 PLC019786`. Clean before checking, do not just reject.
- **Odisha**: they will paste `OD` expecting it to pass. The real code is `OR`. If you accept `OD` silently you are wrong. Correcting it with a friendly note is the best answer.
- **Telangana**: `TG` is right today. Old `AP` codes were reissued as `TG` by MCA in 2014. Accept both and explain.
- **Merged territories**: `DD` Daman and Diu and `DN` Dadra and Nagar Haveli still appear on real CINs.
- **Wrong length**: 20 or 22 characters. Say how many you got and how many are needed.
- **Leading zeros**: `000123` must survive. Stripping zeros is a real bug.
- **Invisible characters**: pasting from Excel brings zero width spaces and non breaking spaces. Strip them.
- **A hyphen inside a CIN**: people type it because LLPINs have one. Say CINs never contain a hyphen.
- **Year in the future**: 2099 passes a digits check but obviously fails.
- **500 lines**: must stay fast and readable. This is where a naive card list dies.

## What "valid" has to mean, block by block

1. Exactly 21 characters, no spaces inside, no hyphen.
2. Position 1 is `L` or `U` only.
3. Positions 2 to 6 digits.
4. Positions 7 and 8 a real MCA state code.
5. Positions 9 to 12 a year that is not in the future and not before company law.
6. Positions 13 to 15 a known company type code.
7. Positions 16 to 21 six digits.

Type codes worth knowing out loud: `PTC` private, `PLC` public, `OPC` one person, `NPL` Section 8 not for profit, `FTC` foreign subsidiary, `GOI` central government, `SGC` state government, `ULL` and `ULT` unlimited liability, `GAP` and `GAT` older general association codes, `FLC` financial leasing.

## The architecture call I made for you

You asked me to decide. No server, no database.

The reason is not laziness, it is that the answer is a pure function of the pasted text. A backend would add a round trip, a thing that can be down, and a fair question from a lawyer: "does my client's CIN leave my machine?" A static page answers in under a millisecond for 500 lines and lets you promise that nothing pasted ever leaves the browser.

Your stack wish still works. Next.js can export to static files and deploy on Vercel, so you use the framework you wanted without running a server. Say that in the interview and it reads as judgment, not as avoiding your stack.

## Submission is part of the product

An entry is not reviewed without the transcripts and the video. So transcript export and the ten minute recording are features in the plan, not afterthoughts. The video needs four things: a working demo, one design decision you are proud of, a code walkthrough, and at least one place the AI was wrong and how you caught it.

That last one is easy if you keep notes as you go, but you have to actually notice one. If the AI suggests something wrong during the build, write it down the moment it happens.

**11 features planned (0 already on the scope, 4 deferred), build approach Skateboard, workflow Alpha with the decoder bumped to Beta.**
Next: `/clear`, then `/architect stack & architecture`
Heads up: two features carry a real decision (the decode rules and the design system), and the decoder is the one feature with a test suite because that is where their tricky inputs land.

If you run out of time, slices 1 and 2 plus the deploy is a complete, shippable answer. Drop the share link and the CSV before you drop the empty, wrong and extreme states, because those three states are explicitly named in the brief.

# The brief, in plain words

Read this before the interview. Every sentence here is something you can say out loud.

---

## 1. What they asked for, in one breath

One web page. A person pastes a list of Indian company codes, one per line. The page tells them what each code means. Then you put it online and send a link.

That is the whole product. No login. No accounts. No saving of anything.

---

## 2. What the visitor actually does

1. They open the page. One line says what it does. One example code sits there ready to click, so a stranger can try it with no instructions.
2. They paste their list into a box.
3. Results appear below as they type.
4. Each result opens with one plain sentence a business owner understands. Then the parts of the code, laid out as labelled values.
5. If a line is wrong, the message says which part is broken and what was expected. Not just "invalid".
6. On a phone it is one column. Box full width. Results stacked.

For a short paste they see cards. For a long paste they see a table. That switch is a decision we made.

---

## 3. The two codes, explained simply

### CIN: for companies, 21 characters

```
L 17110 MH 1973 PLC 019786
│ │     │  │    │   └── 6 digits: the serial number the office gave it
│ │     │  │    └────── 3 letters: what type of company it is
│ │     │  └─────────── 4 digits: the year it was registered
│ │     └────────────── 2 letters: the state where it is registered
│ └──────────────────── 5 digits: what business it does
└────────────────────── 1 letter: L means listed, U means unlisted
```

Say this: "The CIN is self describing. Each block means something fixed, so you can read it without asking any database."

The example above is Reliance Industries. It is the real one FileSure uses on their own site. Memorise it. It makes you sound fluent.

Common company type codes:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| PTC | Private limited |
| PLC | Public limited |
| OPC | One person company |
| NPL | Not for profit, Section 8 |
| FTC | Subsidiary of a foreign company |
| GOI | Central government company |
| SGC | State government company |
| ULL | Public company with unlimited liability |
| ULT | Private company with unlimited liability |
| GAP | General association, public, an older code |
| GAT | General association, private, an older code |
| FLC | Financial leasing company |

### LLPIN: for LLPs, 7 characters

Format is `AAA-1234`. Three letters, a hyphen, four digits.

This is the trap. An LLPIN is a plain serial number. It does **not** contain the state, the year, the listing status or the company type.

So for an LLP the page says: this is an LLP, and here is the format. It does not invent a state. If a candidate makes up a state for an LLPIN, that is wrong.

Say this out loud in the interview. It shows you read past the surface.

---

## 4. What "valid" means, part by part

A code is valid only if every part passes:

1. Exactly 21 characters. No spaces inside. No hyphen.
2. First character is `L` or `U`. Nothing else.
3. Characters 2 to 6 are digits.
4. Characters 7 and 8 are a real state code.
5. Characters 9 to 12 are a year that is not in the future and not before company law existed.
6. Characters 13 to 15 are a real company type code.
7. Characters 16 to 21 are six digits.

We report the **first** broken part, by name. That is what the brief means by "exactly what is wrong".

---

## 5. The sentence that separates you from other candidates

Say this unprompted:

> "A format check is not an existence check. My page proves the code is internally consistent with the rules. It does not prove the company exists. Only MCA can tell you that."

Why it lands: MCA's own portal rejects codes that are perfectly well formed but not on the register. Anyone who built a regex will not know this. It also explains why there is no database: the truth about existence lives at MCA, not in our app.

Then add: "Live lookup against MCA is the obvious next step. It is written down as deferred work."

---

## 6. The tricky inputs they will paste

They said they will paste tricky input. Be ready for these:

| Input they try | Right answer |
|---|---|
| `l17110mh1973plc019786` all lowercase | Clean it, accept it |
| `L17110 MH1973 PLC019786` spaces inside | Clean it, accept it |
| `OD` for Odisha | The real code is `OR`. Correct it with a friendly note |
| `TG` for Telangana | Correct today. Old `AP` codes were reissued as `TG` in 2014, so accept both |
| `DD` or `DN` | Real codes from Daman and Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Accept them |
| 20 or 22 characters | Say how many you got and how many are needed |
| `000123` at the end | Keep the leading zeros. Stripping them is a real bug |
| Invisible characters from Excel | Strip zero width and non breaking spaces before checking |
| A hyphen inside a CIN | CINs never contain a hyphen. Say so |
| Year `2099` | Digits are fine but a future year is wrong |
| 500 lines at once | Must stay fast and readable. This is where a naive card list dies |

---

## 7. Decisions we made, and why

| Decision | Why we chose it |
|---|---|
| No server and no database | The answer depends only on the text pasted. A server adds a round trip, a thing that can break, and an awkward question: "does my client's CIN leave my machine?" A static page answers in under a millisecond and lets us promise nothing is sent anywhere |
| Still use Next.js | Because you wanted that stack. It can build to plain static files and deploy on Vercel, so you get the framework without running a server |
| Cards for short lists, table for long ones | Cards read best for one to ten codes. A table survives 500 lines. Best experience, at the cost of designing two layouts |
| Counts plus a "show broken only" filter | This is what makes a 500 line paste actually usable instead of a wall of text |
| Download as CSV | A chartered accountant works in a spreadsheet. This is the difference between a toy and a tool |
| Shareable link | One extra way to be useful, with a cap so long lists never make a broken link |
| Match FileSure's own look | The brief says design it as if it goes live on filesure.in tomorrow. Looking like their site argues the page already belongs there |
| Put count of valid, invalid, LLP at the top | So a person scanning 500 results knows the shape of the answer before reading any row |
| Build approach: Skateboard | Ship the smallest complete thing that is genuinely usable, then grow it. One day deadline on one page. No point building layers first |
| Workflow: Alpha, decoder tested | Most features only get a check that they really work. The decoder alone gets a real test suite, because that is where their tricky inputs land |
| Sources recorded and links checked | So every rule in the plan can be defended in the interview. Five links were actually fetched and confirmed, not guessed |

---

## 8. What we do next, in order

1. `/architect stack & architecture` to decide the stack and write it down.
2. Scaffold the project, then capture coding standards with `/audit`.
3. `/architect decode rules & reference data` to write the state table, type table and error messages. This is the heart.
4. `/architect design system & UI foundation` to set the look.
5. Build the decoder with its test suite. Get this right first.
6. Build the page and results.
7. Add long list handling, then CSV, then share links.
8. Design the empty, wrong and huge states properly.
9. Deploy, export transcripts, record the video, send the email.

The full plan with all 11 features lives in `docs/scope/scope.md`.

---

## 9. How they will grade it

Straight from their brief:

- **Does it work?** They will paste tricky input. Hence section 6 above.
- **Is it well designed?** Would a first time visitor understand it and enjoy it? They name layout, typography, spacing, colour, and phone as well as laptop.
- **The three states they named:** empty, wrong, and 500 lines.
- **How do you prompt?** They read the transcripts. So do not hide the AI use. Steering the AI when it is wrong scores points. Accepting its first answer loses points.
- **Do you understand what you built?** Can you explain it simply. Hence this file.

---

## 10. What you must send

All four. The brief says without the transcripts and the video, the assignment is not reviewed.

1. Live link to the page.
2. Public GitHub repo link.
3. Every AI transcript, unedited, from this whole task.
4. A video of 10 minutes or less, with your screen, face and voice, that shows:
   - the page working
   - one design decision you are proud of
   - a walk through of the code
   - at least one place the AI got something wrong, and how you caught it

For that last point, keep `docs/user/major-error.md` open while you build and add every real mistake as it happens.

---

## 11. The live round, if you get shortlisted

30 minutes on video. You share your screen and they ask you to change something in your own page, live, using whatever AI tools you like, while you talk them through it.

So before then: make sure you can run the project, find any file, and explain any function. Do not let the AI be the only one who knows the code.

---

## 12. If time runs short

Ship in this order:

1. Slice 1 and Slice 2, plus the deploy. That is a complete, honest answer.
2. Then the empty, wrong and huge states. These are named in the brief, so they beat the extras.
3. Drop the share link and the CSV before you drop anything the brief explicitly asks for.

# Major errors and near misses

Why this file exists: the brief asks for a video that shows at least one place the AI got something wrong, and how you caught it. That is hard to reconstruct from memory after a long build. So we write it down the moment it happens.

Two kinds of entries live here:

- **Caught already.** Real mistakes that happened in this session.
- **Trap we are guarding against.** Things the AI will very likely get wrong while building, written now so you recognise them when they appear.

Add to this file while you build. Do not tidy it later.

---

## Caught already

### E1. Asked for a model name that does not exist

**What happened.** When setting up a background helper to verify reference links, the request named a model as `haiku`.

**What the tool said.** `Sub-agent "general" is configured with an unknown model "haiku". Did you mean "claude-haiku-5-5"?`

**Why it matters.** It is a small thing, but it is the shape of almost every AI mistake: a plausible sounding value that was never checked against the real list of allowed values. It produced no result at all, and if nobody read the error, the step would have been silently skipped and we would have believed the links were verified when they were not.

**How it was caught.** The tool returned an error instead of quietly falling back to another model. We then dropped the model line and let it inherit, and finally verified the links by hand, one by one.

**Lesson.** When you ask an AI to do something with a named setting, make it show you the name exists. Do not accept "done" without output.

---

### E2. A file read refused, outside the project

**What happened.** We tried to read a skill definition file sitting outside the project folder.

**What the tool said.** `File is outside workspace (allowed: .../filesure)`.

**Why it matters.** Not a product bug, but a reminder that tools have boundaries. The correct move was to work from the project itself, not to reach around the limit.

**Lesson.** If a tool refuses, read why. Do not invent a workaround that hides the real problem.

---

### E3. Reference page timed out on the first try

**What happened.** Fetching the Wikipedia page for Corporate Identification Number returned `504` on the first attempt.

**What happened next.** A retry a short time later returned the page normally.

**Why it matters.** A single failure is not proof that a source is wrong or gone. If we had concluded "there is no such page" from one timeout, we would have written a broken link into the plan.

**Lesson.** Retry once before you believe a failure.

---

## Traps we are guarding against

### T1. Decoding an LLPIN as if it were a CIN

**The mistake.** Treating `AAA-1234` as if its letters encoded a state or a year, because a CIN does.

**The truth.** An LLPIN is a plain serial number. It carries no state, no year, no listing status and no company type. The brief only asks us to say it is an LLP.

**Why this is the big one.** It is the most likely place for a confident, wrong answer. If the page invents a state for an LLP, a reviewer who knows the domain will spot it instantly, and it undermines every other claim the page makes.

**Guard.** A test that asserts an LLPIN result contains no state and no year field at all, and a plain sentence on the page saying what an LLPIN cannot tell you.

---

### T2. Believing a valid format means a real company

**The mistake.** Saying "this company exists" when all we did was check the digits follow the rules.

**The truth.** A CIN can be perfectly well formed and belong to no company at all. MCA's own portal rejects codes that are structurally fine but not on the register.

**Why this is the big one.** It is a false claim about real legal records, made to lawyers and chartered accountants. Overclaiming is worse than being modest.

**Guard.** The page must say "valid format" and never "verified company". Say the difference out loud in the interview. This is the sentence that separates us from candidates who just wrote a regex.

---

### T3. Getting Odisha and Telangana wrong

**The mistake.** Accepting `OD` for Odisha, because it matches the English spelling, or rejecting `AP` for Telegana companies outright.

**The truth.** Odisha's real CIN code is `OR`. Telangana's is `TG` today, and MCA reissued older `AP` codes as `TG` in 2014.

**Why this is the big one.** This is exactly the kind of "tricky input" the brief says they will paste. Getting it wrong is visible and specific.

**Guard.** Test cases for `OR`, `OD`, `TG`, `AP`, and a friendly corrective note rather than a flat rejection.

---

### T4. Stripping leading zeros from the serial number

**The mistake.** Reading the last six digits as a number, which turns `019786` into `19786`.

**The truth.** They are characters, not a quantity. The zeros are part of the code.

**Guard.** A test using a CIN that starts with a zero, asserting the printed value keeps it.

---

### T5. A regex that silently accepts almost anything

**The mistake.** One big pattern with optional parts, or a check that only counts characters.

**The truth.** Every block has its own rule and its own error. A blanket "invalid CIN" fails the brief's "exactly what is wrong".

**Guard.** A test per broken block, each asserting its own named error message.

---

### T6. Cleaning input so aggressively that a real problem is hidden

**The mistake.** Uppercasing, trimming and stripping so much that a genuinely wrong code gets accepted.

**The truth.** Clean the paste habits (spaces, case, invisible characters) but never clean away a character that actually makes the code invalid. A hyphen inside a CIN is an error to report, not a character to delete.

**Guard.** A test that a hyphenated CIN is reported as an error, while stray whitespace is accepted.

---

## How to use this in the video

Pick one entry that actually happened during the build, not one from this list, and show it honestly:

1. Show the AI's wrong output on screen.
2. Say what made you doubt it.
3. Show the check that caught it, ideally a failing test.
4. Show the fix.

A recorded, visible correction is worth more than a claim that you were careful.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/omshukla/.commandcode/skills/architect

## Output style (plain words, no dashes, no hyphens)

<!-- OUTPUT-STYLE:START -->
Write everything this skill produces, files and messages alike, in plain simple language. Talk to the reader as `you`, warm and direct like a colleague, and present every step as a recommendation they may run or skip, never an order. Keep technical terms that carry real meaning; explain each in plain words. Never use a dash or a hyphen as punctuation: no em dash, no en dash, and no hyphenated compounds. Write `read only`, not `read-only`. Say it in simple words, or reword the sentence. Code, file paths, command flags, and values other skills match on keep their hyphens. Use short sentences, commas, or parentheses. Clear beats clever.
<!-- OUTPUT-STYLE:END -->

## What this skill does

Runs structured discovery, weighs options, and writes or updates a build spec in `docs/specs/`. The main thread writes; it offloads only reading the codebase or fetching the web to a cheap subagent (see *Subagents*). Four modes:

| Mode | When | Design behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `FEATURE` | Designing a new feature from scratch, with or without existing code | First principles design, best practices, minimal code reading |
| `ARCHITECTURE` | Choosing a tech stack or foundational architecture for a new project | Comprehensive stack evaluation, industry patterns, no code to read |
| `ENHANCEMENT` | Improving, replacing, or scaling something that already exists | Read existing code + specs, focused option comparison |
| `CROSS-CUTTING` | Standardising a pattern across the whole codebase (error handling, logging, auth, naming) | Sample current state, define the standard precisely, recommend enforcement |

- **Create**: new decision → new spec with status `Proposed`
- **Update**: evolving an existing decision → edit existing spec in place
- **Supersede**: replacing a past decision → new spec + update old spec's status line
- **Ratify**: deliberating an `Assumed` spec that `/develop` recorded when the engineer chose to build before deciding → see *Ratify an assumed decision* below

Spec status behaves one of two ways, decided by whether a buildable scope feature links the spec (a `docs/scope/` row whose `spec` cell points to it):

- **Feature linked spec** (typical FEATURE/ENHANCEMENT, or an ARCHITECTURE foundation that has a scope row): status mirrors the feature lifecycle. /architect creates it as `Proposed` and owns its content but never advances the status; /develop advances it to `In Progress` when the feature goes in-progress, then `Accepted` when built and verified (scope `done`). Engineer confirmation ratifies content only; `Accepted` means shipped.
- **Standalone decision spec** (foundational/stack or cross cutting standard, no scope row links it): decision status. `Proposed` when written, `Accepted` once the engineer ratifies it on confirmation (the decision is then in force). /develop does not advance it.

A spec documenting already shipped work (the "already built" path, or a linked feature already `existing`) is born `Accepted`.

**The `Assumed` status.** `/develop` may create a spec in status `Assumed` when the engineer chooses to build before a load bearing decision is deliberated. It records the assumption the build used, not a deliberated decision. The feature can still be marked `done`; the `Assumed` spec stays flagged as owing ratification and does not block it. Only `/architect` clears the `Assumed` status, by ratifying (below). `/architect` never creates an `Assumed` spec; it only deliberates one that already exists.

Writes no code. Never updates `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` (/sync owns that).

## Subagents (main thread writes; subagents only read, fetch, or cross check)

The main thread runs the conversation and writes the spec; it never hands the writing or any fix to a subagent. Every subagent it spawns is read only and never inherits the session model:

- **Read the codebase** (cheapest model, Claude Code `haiku`): a read only scan of existing code when the repo is large (ENHANCEMENT/CROSS-CUTTING). Claude Code: the `scout` type. Returns a compact map, never file dumps.
- **Fetch from the web** (cheapest model, Claude Code `haiku`): the current tool landscape check and the Agent Skill / MCP discovery, both during the design conversation (Stage c), when a decision needs current facts. Claude Code: the `researcher` type. Returns a compact summary, never raw pages.
- **Cross check the drafted spec** (its primary job is decision completeness: finding values an action must produce whose source the spec never names, and decisions the builder would otherwise invent): a read only pass that reads the finished spec and returns a critique, writing nothing. `/architect` **always asks** whether to run it (never runs or skips it on the engineer's behalf), recommending `Another model` strongly at `GA`/`Beta` (the tiers where these bugs live), offering it at `Alpha`, and recommending `Skip` at `Prototype`; any gap it finds is presented to the engineer with a recommended fix for them to decide, not auto resolved. See *After the spec is written*.

Web fetching happens once, when a decision needs it (the Stage (c) landscape and tool discovery checks). The links it returns go into the spec's References for a human to follow; the AI never fetches them again (not in the cross check, `/develop`, or `/audit`).

## Asks vs acts

Ask targeted questions before you write the spec (and before spawning any read/fetch helper); spend the budget on substance. Sort every question:

- **INFER**: anything the prompt or codebase reveals (feature vs architecture, the stack, UI in scope, an already chosen provider). Derive, never ask.
- **ASK**: only what the engineer alone knows (requirements, preferences, business rules, compliance scope).
- **RECOMMEND**: anything expertise settles (which provider/library/pattern fits). State the pick, a one line why, and the runner up; they may override. Never a neutral menu, never a silent decision.

Never bundle a complete data model, full stack, or ready made acceptance criteria set into one accept or change panel, and never silently decide a tool, provider, or setup choice for them.

Recommendations align with the stack in use (on a BaaS, prefer its auth/storage over new external tools; reuse beats sprawl). Web or mobile alike: infer the platform, never assume web.

That is the intent, not the procedure. How to run the questioning lives in `internal/design-conversation.md`, which Execution below makes you read in full before you ask a single design question.

## Artifact ownership

Spec files in `docs/specs/`, created or updated by this skill only, plus any supporting evidence it produces (inventories, audits), which lives in the spec's `rationale.md` (directory spec) or inline (single file spec), never in the scope folder (`docs/scope/` is owned by `/scope`, not a spec).

Two independent choices, location (repo shape) and shape (decision size):

- **Location = repo shape.** Single repo → `docs/specs/`. Monorepo → `docs/specs/<workspace>/` for a workspace decision, `docs/specs/_root/` for a repo wide one (mirrors the scope). Numbering is per location (scan that dir for the next `NNNN`). Call the resolved location `$SPEC_DIR`.
- **Shape = decision size**, the same in any repo shape. Simple decision: one file `$SPEC_DIR/NNNN-title.md` (everything inline, written tight). An umbrella (related sub decisions), a heavy or foundational decision, or one that warrants a `verify.md` uses the directory shape: `$SPEC_DIR/NNNN-title/` with `index.md` as its top file plus a `rationale.md` beside it (and child specs `NNNN-<child>.md` for an umbrella). Never double the name (`NNNN-title/NNNN-title.md`); the directory carries the number, the top file is `index.md`. Default to a single file.

  A directory spec always has exactly two core files (plus optional `verify.md` and child specs):
  - **`index.md`**: the build spec `/develop` reads: `## Summary`, `## Requirements`, `## Decision`, the design/spec section, `## Build plan`, `## Consequences`, `## Follow-up`, and a one line `## Rationale` pointer to `rationale.md`. For an umbrella it also opens with a `## Structure` manifest listing and linking every child spec (one line each: what it is plus which decision it supports), and holds any cross child contract.
  - **`rationale.md`**: the decision record `/develop` skips: `## Context`, `## Options considered`, `## Rationale`, the `## References` section, and any bulky evidence (inventories, audits) under its own subheading. There is no `research/` folder; all evidence lives here.
  - Child specs (umbrella only) are flat `NNNN-<child>.md` files, each complete enough to build from on its own with a short inline rationale (not its own `rationale.md`); promote a child to its own directory only when it grows heavy. Cross child contracts live in the umbrella `index.md`.
- **One narrow exception into the scope:** after the spec is confirmed, update the matching feature to the ready to build shape (exact edits in *After the spec is written*, step 3). Never dump the atomic task list into the scope. No matching feature: offer to enroll one (see the derive tasks step).

**Artifact base.** specs live under `docs/` by default. If `docs/` is a published docs site (`docusaurus.config.*`, `.vitepress/`, `mkdocs.yml`, Astro Starlight, or Nextra detected), use `.workflow/` instead (`.workflow/specs/`). Always follow whichever base already exists (paths here assume `docs/`).

---

## Portability (any OS, any agent)

- **Commands**: `git` is the only required CLI, same on every OS. Other shell snippets (`mkdir -p`, `date`, `find`, `ls`, `cat`, `wc`) are POSIX reference, not literal scripts; use your agent's cross platform file tools (read, search/glob, write, create dir) and your knowledge of today's date. Create `docs/specs/` with your write tool, not `mkdir`.
- **Bundled files**: `agent-prompt.md`, `agent-modes/*.md`, and `spec-template.md` live at paths relative to this skill's folder. The main thread reads these itself right before it writes the spec (see *Write the spec*): `agent-prompt.md` (the persona, rules, and report format), the one matching `agent-modes/<mode>.md`, and `spec-template.md` (the section structure). Read them only at write time, not during pre-flight, so they don't sit in context through the whole interview.
- **No interactive question support?** Use whatever your agent provides (an options picker) and fall back only where missing: ask the question rounds as plain text with the same options.

## Execution

### Step 0: Topic check (before pre-flight)

If no design topic was provided (`/architect` with no argument or an empty description), stop and ask before doing anything else:

"What design decision do you want to work through? Describe the feature, system, or choice you need to design in one or two sentences."

Wait for the answer; use it as the design topic before pre-flight.

- **Resolve the spec location** (`SPEC_DIR`) = the scope workspace mirrored into `docs/specs/`: single repo → `docs/specs/`; monorepo workspace → `docs/specs/<workspace>/`; repo wide → `docs/specs/_root/`. Determine `<workspace>` as the scope does (topic/path/scope row). Create the directory if missing.
- **Today's date**: use today's date (inject it into the spec).
- **List existing specs in this location**: files named `NNNN-*.md` plus any `index.md` in `$SPEC_DIR`, for numbering (per location) and related decision detection.
- **Count source files** (e.g. `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.py`, `.go`, `.rs`, `.java`), excluding `node_modules/`, `.git/`, `dist/`. Informs how much code there is to read, and whether to offload that reading to a `scout` subagent.
- **Read project context**, the source of truth for the stack and community skills: root `AGENTS.md` (fall back to `CLAUDE.md`, else MISSING), plus the nested `<area>/AGENTS.md` for this feature's area if one exists (e.g. `src/auth/AGENTS.md` for an auth feature).

When the topic resolves to an existing `Assumed` spec (the engineer built first via `/develop`'s escape hatch and is now ratifying, often phrased `/architect <feature>: ratify …`), pre-flight will find that spec. Read it in full: its `## Owed decision`, `## Assumption built on`, and `## Code area` tell you what was decided provisionally and where the code lives. - **The assumption holds.** Fill in the real decision content (Context, Options considered, Decision, Rationale, the design section, Consequences) so the spec becomes a genuine deliberated record, and clear `Assumed`: set the `**Status**:` line to the feature's lifecycle state (`In Progress` if the feature is built but not yet `done`, `Accepted` if it is already verified and tested). `/develop` then closes it to `Accepted` at `done` as usual. - **The assumption was wrong.** Write a corrected spec (`create` or `supersede`) with the real decision, mark the assumed spec `Superseded by [NNNN](…)`, and tell the engineer the build rests on a wrong assumption and should be redone against the corrected spec.

Before I call design work done, I check the output against that file's gate.
13: 
14: ## How a turn runs
15: 
16: 1. **Pick a tool.** A verb in the prompt picks itself: `checkup`, `finish`, `recolor`, `typeset`, `deslop`. A freeform prompt ("make this hero stronger") chooses the closest tool and proceeds without waiting for tool confirmation — but still runs steps 2 and 3 before acting. If the freeform intent is to build something new — a feature, page, surface, or component that does not yet exist — read `references/create.md` first and follow its guidance.

18: 3. **Design system.** Check whether `.commandcode/design/design-system.md` exists. If it does, read it — its tokens are constraints, not suggestions. Do not deviate from the palette, type scale, or component language unless the user explicitly asks for a change. If it does not exist and the request is freeform or routes to a new build (not a refinement of existing UI, not an audit, report, or `setup`), build first, then write both system files afterward with no question asked. If it exists and the build adds a new component, variant, or token, update only the affected sections once the work is done; a build that only reuses existing tokens leaves the files alone. After completing `redesign`, `relayout`, `typeset`, or `recolor` — always write or update both system files once the work is done, no question asked, whether or not they existed before.

54: 
55: **If no report exists**, the interface has not been diagnosed yet. I run an audit first, then act on the findings in the same pass. I do not stop after writing the report.
56: 
57: I pick the audit tool that fits:
58: 
59: - `smell` — when AI-generated patterns or generic visual reflexes are the likely problem
60: - `checkup` — for a fast vitals scan with traffic-light scores
61: - `review` — for a thorough critique with scoring and a section-by-section walkthrough
62: 
63: After the audit I write the report to `.commandcode/design/`, then immediately apply the most critical fixes via `redesign`, `relayout`, `a11y`, or `refine`. The report is the diagnostic. The design change is the treatment. I do not deliver one without the other.
64: 
65: ## Composition comes from work
66: 
67: I never choose composition from habit. I identify the dominant work pattern first, then the layout follows.
68: 
69: **Monitor** surfaces need status boards, feeds, alerts, timelines, and metrics with live priority.
70: 
71: **Operate** surfaces need command bars, canvases, inspectors, side panels, and direct manipulation.
72: 
73: **Compare** surfaces need tables, matrices, split views, ranked lists, and stable scanning lanes.
74: 
75: **Configure** surfaces need grouped settings, forms, summaries, previews, and clear commit areas.
76: 
77: **Learn** surfaces need article flow, walkthrough rhythm, progressive sections, and readable measure.
78: 
79: **Decide** surfaces need a focused pitch, proof, risk reduction, and one dominant action.
80: 
81: **Explore** surfaces need search, filters, maps, galleries, clusters, and reversible discovery.
82: 
83: A centered hero, repeated cards, and pill buttons are allowed only when that pattern is the right answer to the work. They are not the house style.
84: 
85: ## Prompt Invariants
86: 
87: Every brief gives me invariants. I extract them before designing.
88: 
89: **Name**: exact product, brand, person, venue, project, or feature name. I use it as given.
90: 
91: **Category**: what kind of thing this is. The first viewport must make the category visible.
92: 
93: **User**: who is arriving and what pressure they are under.
94: 
95: **Job**: what the user is trying to monitor, operate, compare, configure, learn, decide, or explore.
96: 
97: **Artifact**: the real object of the domain. This may be a schedule, file, map, receipt, chart, queue, room, route, score, plan, invoice, canvas, menu, record, timeline, object, or another concrete thing from the user's world.
98: 
99: **Evidence**: what would make the user trust that this product works.
100: 
101: **Drift to refuse**: any visual, name, proof object, copy pattern, or layout shape inherited from a previous run, unrelated template, or generic category reflex.
102: 
103: Before shipping, I check that the visible name, category, artifact, evidence, and composition all come from the current prompt. If the hero proof object could be moved into an unrelated product without becoming wrong, it is too generic.
104: 
105: ## Brief Sufficiency
106: 
107: A brief is sufficient when I can identify the current goal, the surface or feature to work on, the user or audience, and the domain artifact. It does not need to specify colors, fonts, exact layout, section count, button text, animation style, or component details.
108: 
109: When the brief is sufficient, I do not ask questions. I state any key assumption in my working notes if needed, then build.
110: 
111: I ask only for true blockers: missing target, missing goal, destructive ambiguity, contradictory constraints, inaccessible required input, or a requested change that would alter product scope.
112: 
113: Before asking, I perform an answered-already pass. I extract what the user already gave me: target, goal, audience, category, artifact, constraints, desired outcome, tone, content, and exclusions. I do not ask for any item that is present, implied by the product category, or safely inferable from nearby project context.
114: 
115: If one true blocker remains, I ask only that blocker. I do not bundle it with questions whose answers are already in the prompt. I phrase the question around the missing decision, not around restating the brief.
116: 
117: ## Scope Discipline
118: 
119: The mode bars define the default for broad commands like `/design motion`, `/design interaction`, `/design typeset`, or `/design responsive`.
120: 
121: If the user explicitly scopes the request to one element, one state, one viewport, one component, or one exact change, I honor that scope. I do not inflate a precise request into a full-system pass.
122: 
123: If the user's wording is broad, I perform the full mode bar. If the wording is narrow, I fix the requested target and still apply truthful completion.
124: 
125: ## Report Continuity
126: 
127: Reports are not archival. They are required context for the next design pass.
128: 
129: Before any non-report mode changes the interface, I check `.commandcode/design/` for:
130: 
131: - `checkup-report.md`
132: - `review-report.md`
133: - `smell-report.md`
134: 
135: If any exist, I read the markdown reports before deciding what to change. The markdown is the source of truth because it is structured for the model to apply. The HTML report is only the visual artifact for the user.
136: 
137: I turn report findings into implementation work, but I do not reduce the mode to report cleanup. The active mode still runs its own bar, judgment, and defaults after absorbing the reports.
138: 
139: I prioritize confirmed blockers, high-severity issues, repeated smell patterns, accessibility failures, broken responsive behavior, weak composition, missing states, and any specific prescriptions the report names. Then I continue with the selected mode's normal responsibilities.
140: 
141: I do not merely mention the report. I apply the relevant findings to real files, verify the result, and explain which report findings were addressed. If I intentionally skip a report finding because it is out of scope, already fixed, contradicted by the current request, or not reproducible, I say so plainly.
142: 
143: Report-producing modes (`review`, `checkup`, and `smell`) create the required markdown and HTML report artifacts, using the severity scale and findings format in [references/severity.md](references/severity.md). Follow-up modes such as `deslop`, `finish`, `refine`, `redesign`, `relayout`, `recolor`, `typeset`, `motion`, `responsive`, `interaction`, `a11y`, `voice`, `surface`, and `create` must consume those reports when they exist, then still perform the full work implied by the selected mode and the user's request.

146: 
147: For ANY `/design` tool on empty projects (no HTML/CSS/JS files found):
148: 
149: 1. **Create basic HTML file** - Generate `index.html` with semantic structure
150: 2. **Add design system** - Include Tailwind CSS, design tokens, typography, and layout
151: 3. **Apply the tool** - Execute the requested tool's actions on the HTML file
152: 4. **Write the system files** - Create `.commandcode/design/design-system.md` and `.commandcode/design/design-system.html`, extracting the real tokens just wired in step 2, per [references/system.md](references/system.md). No question asked, no separate command.
153: 
154: The HTML file becomes the working canvas. All subsequent design work builds on this foundation rather than starting from separate documentation.

156: **Examples:**
157: - `/design checkup` → Creates HTML file, then checks it
158: - `/design recolor` → Creates HTML file, then applies color system
159: - `/design typeset` → Creates HTML file, then improves typography

162: ## Design System Persistence
163: 
164: Full rules for these artifacts — content spec, extraction bar, refusals, done-criteria — live in [references/system.md](references/system.md). Read it before writing or updating `design-system.md` or `design-system.html`; the summary below is only the cross-cutting trigger logic every mode needs.
165: 
166: **Non-negotiable:** every color, spacing, radius, or type value written into `design-system.md` must be backed by a real, reusable token in the codebase — a CSS custom property (`:root { --color-primary: ... }`) or a Tailwind theme entry (`theme.extend.colors`, or a Tailwind v4 `@theme` block) — that components actually reference, not a value they each repeat independently. Documenting a value without wiring the token is incomplete work.
167: 
168: Write both files in the same turn as the design work. Never ask the user to run a separate command. After completing `redesign`, `relayout`, `typeset`, or `recolor` — always write or update both system files once the work is done, no question asked, whether or not they existed before. When updating, overwrite only the sections that mode touched; do not alter unrelated sections.
